newsitem.title: USA: Sprint says Internet snags mostly cleared.
newsitem.headline: Sprint says Internet snags mostly cleared.

text.p: A problem at an Internet service provider (ISP) in Virginia triggered a massive logjam on the Internet Friday, but the trouble was cleared up later in the day, Sprint Corp. said.

A customer of MAI Network Services, a McLean, Va.-based Internet provider that is among 900 companies that buy wholesale access to the Net from Sprint, entered 10,000 duplicate routes to the Internet backbone -- one of the trunk lines of the Net -- at one time.
That caused massive access delays for an undetermined number of users, Sprint spokesman Russ Robinson said.

"This is what caused the disruption in traffic," Robinson said in an interview. "We spent the morning notifying other ISPs of the situation and began cleaning up the router tables (which control data flow between the Internet and ISPs)," he said.
Full service to the Internet was restored by late afternoon, Robinson said.

Robinson said Sprint, which sells the access but does not manage the Internet, is still looking at how the situation developed. "This type of thing (a router tie-up) happens all of the time, but never on this scale," he said.
A typical router can handle 46,000 entries seeking access to the Internet, Robinson said.
"Adding 10,000 at one time suddenly pushed that up to 56,000, and some of our older routers just stopped working completely (beacuse of the overload)," Robinson explained.

MAI Network Services spokesman Vince Bono said the problem began when one of its small corporate customers tried logging on to both MAI Network and another ISP at the same time without letting either ISP know.
Bono said that the customer had not configured its setup properly, which led to the router problem.
MAI "pulled the plug" on its service as soon as it realized what was happening. It had not restored service to its 100 customers as of late Friday.
